the drought in the Maya lowlands was of short duration (125 days) and that the decrease in precipitation was not catastrophic (40%).

the impact of drought on maize production and its potential effect on ancient Maya society during the last half millennium.

the drought of the last half of first millennium ce did not result in a significant decline in maize cropping success.
the drought in Yucatán Peninsula was not a major cause of the decline of the Classic Maya civilization.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the ancient Maya had the ability to adapt to climate variability.
the drought in the last half of first millennium ce was not sufficient to cause a collapse of ancient Maya civilization.

the climate of the last half millennium of Maya civilization was generally wet, but there was no evidence of a significant change in the climate that would have had an adverse impact on the cropping of maize.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the climate-based explanation of the collapse of the Maya civilization is still a conjecture and that it needs to be supported with more rigorous quantitative assessment of the effects of climate on maize cropping.
, to the extent that climate change is a factor in the demise of ancient Maya, the effect is likely to be gradual and not sudden.
, in general, climate is not the main cause of the ‘collapse of ancient Maya civilization’.
